Schedules A/B through J - assets, debts, income, expenses.

Statement of Financial Affairs - Form 107.

Means Test - Form 122A-1 (Chapter 7) or 122C-1 (Chapter 13).

Statement of Intention - Form 108 (Chapter 7 only).

Chapter 13 Plan - Form 113 (Chapter 13 only).

Credit counseling certificate - dated within 180 days before filing.

Pay stubs - 60 days before filing (or Form 121 certification if none).

Tax return - most recent year's federal tax return; must be provided to the trustee at least 7 days before 341 meeting.

Creditor matrix - mailing addresses in the court's required format.

New Jersey districts may require local cover sheets and additional local forms. See Chapter 7 checklist and Chapter 13 checklist.

New Jersey 341 Meeting of Creditors

After filing, the court sets a 341 meeting (meeting of creditors) 20-40 days out. In New Jersey:

Attendance is mandatory. Missing the 341 is a leading cause of dismissal.

Format varies. Many New Jersey districts now use telephonic or video 341 meetings post-2020; some have returned to in-person. Check the notice carefully.

You answer under oath. The trustee asks standard questions about your schedules, income, and financial situation.

Duration: Typically 5-15 minutes for a no-asset Chapter 7; longer for contested matters or Chapter 13.

Bring photo ID and Social Security card (or W-2 showing SSN).

New Jersey Federal Bankruptcy Data

New Jersey's federal bankruptcy courts handle both attorney-filed and pro se cases under the same rules. The FJC numbers below give you a sense of New Jersey docket scale and outcomes.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,580 consumer bankruptcy cases from New Jersey's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 752697.3%2.7%

Chapter 131,05431.0%68.8%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Bankruptcy Petition Preparers (BPPs) in New Jersey

BPPs are non-lawyers who type bankruptcy petitions for a fee under 11 U.S.C. Section 110. In New Jersey:

A BPP may type the forms you direct but cannot advise you on the law.

BPP fees are regulated; in most districts capped at $200-$225.

The BPP must sign the petition and disclose their identity (name, address, SSN or EIN).

BPPs are subject to sanctions for legal advice or for failing to disclose.

BPPs differ from licensed attorneys in that they cannot: (a) advise on exemptions, (b) advise on chapter choice, (c) represent you in court, (d) draft a Chapter 13 plan.

A BPP is useful if you can read and complete the forms yourself but want help with formatting. A BPP is not a substitute for legal advice. See full BPP guide.

Common New Jersey Pro Se Mistakes

Forgetting a creditor. Missing a creditor from the matrix can mean that debt is not discharged.

Undervaluing assets. The trustee will check; undervaluation looks like concealment.

Overlooking the New Jersey exemption election. Schedule C must affirmatively claim each exemption.

Missing the 60-day pay advice rule. Employer-issued pay stubs for 60 days pre-filing are required.

Filing without credit counseling certificate. The certificate must pre-date the petition.

Missing Rule 9037 redactions. Full SSNs, account numbers, and minor names trigger clerk alerts and must be re-filed.

See full mistake list.

## File Bankruptcy Without a Lawyer in New Mexico [2026]: Courts, Fees, and Procedure
Source: https://filebankruptcywithoutlawyer.com/states/new-mexico.html

← filebankruptcywithoutlawyer.com home

File Bankruptcy Without a Lawyer in New Mexico [2026]: Courts, Fees, and Procedure

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for New Mexico residents.

Filing Bankruptcy Pro Se in New Mexico - Quick Orientation

Bankruptcy is federal. All New Mexico pro se filings go to a federal bankruptcy court, not a state court. You retain the 28 U.S.C. Section 1654 right to self-representation for individual cases (Chapter 7 and Chapter 13). Corporations and LLCs cannot file pro se per Rowland.

ItemNew Mexico Detail

Bankruptcy districtsDistrict of New Mexico

Main courthouses500 Gold Ave SW, Albuquerque, NM 87102

Filing notesSingle district; Albuquerque courthouse.

Chapter 7 filing fee$338 (2026)

Chapter 13 filing fee$313 (2026)

Chapter 11 filing fee$1,738 (consumer)

Venue - Where to File in New Mexico

Federal bankruptcy venue is governed by 28 U.S.C. Section 1408. File in the district where you have:

Domicile, residence, or principal place of business for the greater part of the 180 days immediately preceding filing, OR

Principal assets for the same period, OR

An affiliated pending case.

New Mexico venue note: Single district; Albuquerque courthouse.

New Mexico Filing Fees (2026) and Fee Waivers

ChapterFiling FeeMiscellaneous

Chapter 7$338Waiver possible if income < 150% of poverty line (Form 103B)

Chapter 13$313Installment payments available (up to 4 per Rule 1006)

Chapter 11 (consumer)$1,738No waiver; installments possible

Chapter 12 (family farmer)$278Installments possible

Credit counseling$15-$50Pre-filing, 180-day validity, sliding scale available

Debtor education$15-$50Post-filing, pre-discharge

Additional fees (amendments, motions, reopening) are set by the U.S. Judicial Conference and published on uscourts.gov.

New Mexico E-Filing vs Paper Filing for Pro Se

Most New Mexico bankruptcy courts require paper filing for pro se debtors. CM/ECF (the electronic filing system) is generally reserved for licensed attorneys admitted to the district, though some districts offer limited pro se e-filing with pre-approval.

Practical New Mexico pro se filing workflow:

Download all national Official Forms from uscourts.gov.

Download the New Mexico district's Local Rules and local forms from the district's website.

Complete forms. Wet-ink signature on originals where required.

Make 3 copies (court, trustee, your file).

Pay the filing fee (cashier's check, money order, or in-person credit card if court accepts).

File in person or by mail to the clerk's office at one of the courthouses above.

See DIY bankruptcy walkthrough.

Pay stubs - 60 days before filing (or Form 121 certification if none).

## File Bankruptcy Without a Lawyer in Ohio [2026]: Courts, Fees, and Procedure
Source: https://filebankruptcywithoutlawyer.com/states/ohio.html

← filebankruptcywithoutlawyer.com home

File Bankruptcy Without a Lawyer in Ohio [2026]: Courts, Fees, and Procedure

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Ohio residents.

Filing Bankruptcy Pro Se in Ohio - Quick Orientation

Bankruptcy is federal. All Ohio pro se filings go to a federal bankruptcy court, not a state court. You retain the 28 U.S.C. Section 1654 right to self-representation for individual cases (Chapter 7 and Chapter 13). Corporations and LLCs cannot file pro se per Rowland.

ItemOhio Detail

Bankruptcy districtsNorthern and Southern Districts

Main courthouses801 W. Superior, Cleveland (OHN); 170 N. High St., Columbus + 120 W. 3rd St., Dayton (OHS)

Filing notes2 districts; heavy consumer docket.

Chapter 7 filing fee$338 (2026)

Chapter 13 filing fee$313 (2026)

Chapter 11 filing fee$1,738 (consumer)

Venue - Where to File in Ohio

Federal bankruptcy venue is governed by 28 U.S.C. Section 1408. File in the district where you have:

Domicile, residence, or principal place of business for the greater part of the 180 days immediately preceding filing, OR

Principal assets for the same period, OR

An affiliated pending case.

Ohio venue note: 2 districts; heavy consumer docket.

Ohio Filing Fees (2026) and Fee Waivers

ChapterFiling FeeMiscellaneous

Chapter 7$338Waiver possible if income < 150% of poverty line (Form 103B)

Chapter 13$313Installment payments available (up to 4 per Rule 1006)

Chapter 11 (consumer)$1,738No waiver; installments possible

Chapter 12 (family farmer)$278Installments possible

Credit counseling$15-$50Pre-filing, 180-day validity, sliding scale available

Debtor education$15-$50Post-filing, pre-discharge

Additional fees (amendments, motions, reopening) are set by the U.S. Judicial Conference and published on uscourts.gov.

Ohio E-Filing vs Paper Filing for Pro Se

Most Ohio bankruptcy courts require paper filing for pro se debtors. CM/ECF (the electronic filing system) is generally reserved for licensed attorneys admitted to the district, though some districts offer limited pro se e-filing with pre-approval.

Practical Ohio pro se filing workflow:

Download all national Official Forms from uscourts.gov.

Download the Ohio district's Local Rules and local forms from the district's website.

Complete forms. Wet-ink signature on originals where required.

Make 3 copies (court, trustee, your file).

Pay the filing fee (cashier's check, money order, or in-person credit card if court accepts).

File in person or by mail to the clerk's office at one of the courthouses above.

See DIY bankruptcy walkthrough.

Required Forms for Ohio Pro Se Filing

Every pro se Chapter 7 or 13 filing in Ohio includes the following minimum set:

Voluntary Petition - Form 101 (individual) or 201 (entity, but pro se not allowed).

Schedules A/B through J - assets, debts, income, expenses.

Statement of Financial Affairs - Form 107.

Means Test - Form 122A-1 (Chapter 7) or 122C-1 (Chapter 13).

Statement of Intention - Form 108 (Chapter 7 only).

Chapter 13 Plan - Form 113 (Chapter 13 only).

Credit counseling certificate - dated within 180 days before filing.

Pay stubs - 60 days before filing (or Form 121 certification if none).

Tax return - most recent year's federal tax return; must be provided to the trustee at least 7 days before 341 meeting.

Creditor matrix - mailing addresses in the court's required format.

Ohio districts may require local cover sheets and additional local forms. See Chapter 7 checklist and Chapter 13 checklist.

Ohio 341 Meeting of Creditors

After filing, the court sets a 341 meeting (meeting of creditors) 20-40 days out. In Ohio:

Attendance is mandatory. Missing the 341 is a leading cause of dismissal.

Format varies. Many Ohio districts now use telephonic or video 341 meetings post-2020; some have returned to in-person. Check the notice carefully.

You answer under oath. The trustee asks standard questions about your schedules, income, and financial situation.

Duration: Typically 5-15 minutes for a no-asset Chapter 7; longer for contested matters or Chapter 13.

Bring photo ID and Social Security card (or W-2 showing SSN).

Ohio Federal Bankruptcy Data

Ohio's federal bankruptcy courts handle both attorney-filed and pro se cases under the same rules. The FJC numbers below give you a sense of Ohio docket scale and outcomes.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 3,971 consumer bankruptcy cases from Ohio's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 73,53597.7%1.8%

Chapter 1343651.1%48.9%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Bankruptcy Petition Preparers (BPPs) in Ohio

BPPs are non-lawyers who type bankruptcy petitions for a fee under 11 U.S.C. Section 110. In Ohio:

A BPP may type the forms you direct but cannot advise you on the law.

BPP fees are regulated; in most districts capped at $200-$225.

The BPP must sign the petition and disclose their identity (name, address, SSN or EIN).

BPPs are subject to sanctions for legal advice or for failing to disclose.

BPPs differ from licensed attorneys in that they cannot: (a) advise on exemptions, (b) advise on chapter choice, (c) represent you in court, (d) draft a Chapter 13 plan.

A BPP is useful if you can read and complete the forms yourself but want help with formatting. A BPP is not a substitute for legal advice. See full BPP guide.

Common Ohio Pro Se Mistakes

Forgetting a creditor. Missing a creditor from the matrix can mean that debt is not discharged.

Undervaluing assets. The trustee will check; undervaluation looks like concealment.

Overlooking the Ohio exemption election. Schedule C must affirmatively claim each exemption.

Missing the 60-day pay advice rule. Employer-issued pay stubs for 60 days pre-filing are required.

Filing without credit counseling certificate. The certificate must pre-date the petition.

Missing Rule 9037 redactions. Full SSNs, account numbers, and minor names trigger clerk alerts and must be re-filed.

See full mistake list.

Related Ohio Resources

Chapter 7 pro se walkthrough

Chapter 13 pro se walkthrough

Filing fees

Petition software options

Credit counseling

Common mistakes

Voluntary Petition - Form 101 (individual) or 201 (entity, but pro se not allowed).

Schedules A/B through J - assets, debts, income, expenses.

Statement of Financial Affairs - Form 107.

Means Test - Form 122A-1 (Chapter 7) or 122C-1 (Chapter 13).

Statement of Intention - Form 108 (Chapter 7 only).

Chapter 13 Plan - Form 113 (Chapter 13 only).

Credit counseling certificate - dated within 180 days before filing.

Pay stubs - 60 days before filing (or Form 121 certification if none).

Tax return - most recent year's federal tax return; must be provided to the trustee at least 7 days before 341 meeting.

Creditor matrix - mailing addresses in the court's required format.

Rhode Island districts may require local cover sheets and additional local forms. See Chapter 7 checklist and Chapter 13 checklist.

Rhode Island 341 Meeting of Creditors

After filing, the court sets a 341 meeting (meeting of creditors) 20-40 days out. In Rhode Island:

Attendance is mandatory. Missing the 341 is a leading cause of dismissal.

Format varies. Many Rhode Island districts now use telephonic or video 341 meetings post-2020; some have returned to in-person. Check the notice carefully.

You answer under oath. The trustee asks standard questions about your schedules, income, and financial situation.

Duration: Typically 5-15 minutes for a no-asset Chapter 7; longer for contested matters or Chapter 13.

Bring photo ID and Social Security card (or W-2 showing SSN).

Bankruptcy Petition Preparers (BPPs) in Rhode Island

BPPs are non-lawyers who type bankruptcy petitions for a fee under 11 U.S.C. Section 110. In Rhode Island:

A BPP may type the forms you direct but cannot advise you on the law.

BPP fees are regulated; in most districts capped at $200-$225.

The BPP must sign the petition and disclose their identity (name, address, SSN or EIN).

BPPs are subject to sanctions for legal advice or for failing to disclose.

BPPs differ from licensed attorneys in that they cannot: (a) advise on exemptions, (b) advise on chapter choice, (c) represent you in court, (d) draft a Chapter 13 plan.

A BPP is useful if you can read and complete the forms yourself but want help with formatting. A BPP is not a substitute for legal advice. See full BPP guide.

Common Rhode Island Pro Se Mistakes

Forgetting a creditor. Missing a creditor from the matrix can mean that debt is not discharged.

Undervaluing assets. The trustee will check; undervaluation looks like concealment.

Overlooking the Rhode Island exemption election. Schedule C must affirmatively claim each exemption.

Missing the 60-day pay advice rule. Employer-issued pay stubs for 60 days pre-filing are required.

Filing without credit counseling certificate. The certificate must pre-date the petition.

Missing Rule 9037 redactions. Full SSNs, account numbers, and minor names trigger clerk alerts and must be re-filed.

See full mistake list.

Chapter 13 pro se walkthrough

## File Bankruptcy Without a Lawyer in South Carolina [2026]: Courts, Fees, and Procedure
Source: https://filebankruptcywithoutlawyer.com/states/south-carolina.html

← filebankruptcywithoutlawyer.com home

File Bankruptcy Without a Lawyer in South Carolina [2026]: Courts, Fees, and Procedure

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for South Carolina residents.

Filing Bankruptcy Pro Se in South Carolina - Quick Orientation

Bankruptcy is federal. All South Carolina pro se filings go to a federal bankruptcy court, not a state court. You retain the 28 U.S.C. Section 1654 right to self-representation for individual cases (Chapter 7 and Chapter 13). Corporations and LLCs cannot file pro se per Rowland.

ItemSouth Carolina Detail

Bankruptcy districtsDistrict of South Carolina (Bankruptcy Administrator)

Main courthouses1100 Laurel St., Columbia, SC 29201

Filing notesSingle district; Columbia; Bankruptcy Administrator.

Chapter 7 filing fee$338 (2026)

Chapter 13 filing fee$313 (2026)

Chapter 11 filing fee$1,738 (consumer)

Venue - Where to File in South Carolina

Federal bankruptcy venue is governed by 28 U.S.C. Section 1408. File in the district where you have:

Domicile, residence, or principal place of business for the greater part of the 180 days immediately preceding filing, OR

Principal assets for the same period, OR

An affiliated pending case.

South Carolina venue note: Single district; Columbia; Bankruptcy Administrator.

South Carolina Filing Fees (2026) and Fee Waivers

ChapterFiling FeeMiscellaneous

Chapter 7$338Waiver possible if income < 150% of poverty line (Form 103B)

Chapter 13$313Installment payments available (up to 4 per Rule 1006)

Chapter 11 (consumer)$1,738No waiver; installments possible

Chapter 12 (family farmer)$278Installments possible

Credit counseling$15-$50Pre-filing, 180-day validity, sliding scale available

Debtor education$15-$50Post-filing, pre-discharge

Additional fees (amendments, motions, reopening) are set by the U.S. Judicial Conference and published on uscourts.gov.

South Carolina E-Filing vs Paper Filing for Pro Se

Most South Carolina bankruptcy courts require paper filing for pro se debtors. CM/ECF (the electronic filing system) is generally reserved for licensed attorneys admitted to the district, though some districts offer limited pro se e-filing with pre-approval.

Practical South Carolina pro se filing workflow:

Download all national Official Forms from uscourts.gov.

Download the South Carolina district's Local Rules and local forms from the district's website.

Complete forms. Wet-ink signature on originals where required.

Make 3 copies (court, trustee, your file).

Pay the filing fee (cashier's check, money order, or in-person credit card if court accepts).

File in person or by mail to the clerk's office at one of the courthouses above.

See DIY bankruptcy walkthrough.

Required Forms for South Carolina Pro Se Filing

Every pro se Chapter 7 or 13 filing in South Carolina includes the following minimum set:

Voluntary Petition - Form 101 (individual) or 201 (entity, but pro se not allowed).

Schedules A/B through J - assets, debts, income, expenses.

Statement of Financial Affairs - Form 107.

Means Test - Form 122A-1 (Chapter 7) or 122C-1 (Chapter 13).

Statement of Intention - Form 108 (Chapter 7 only).

Chapter 13 Plan - Form 113 (Chapter 13 only).

Credit counseling certificate - dated within 180 days before filing.

Pay stubs - 60 days before filing (or Form 121 certification if none).

Tax return - most recent year's federal tax return; must be provided to the trustee at least 7 days before 341 meeting.

Creditor matrix - mailing addresses in the court's required format.

South Carolina districts may require local cover sheets and additional local forms. See Chapter 7 checklist and Chapter 13 checklist.

South Carolina 341 Meeting of Creditors

After filing, the court sets a 341 meeting (meeting of creditors) 20-40 days out. In South Carolina:

Attendance is mandatory. Missing the 341 is a leading cause of dismissal.

Format varies. Many South Carolina districts now use telephonic or video 341 meetings post-2020; some have returned to in-person. Check the notice carefully.

You answer under oath. The trustee asks standard questions about your schedules, income, and financial situation.

Duration: Typically 5-15 minutes for a no-asset Chapter 7; longer for contested matters or Chapter 13.

Bring photo ID and Social Security card (or W-2 showing SSN).

South Carolina Federal Bankruptcy Data

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 635 consumer bankruptcy cases from South Carolina's federal bankruptcy courts.

## File Bankruptcy Without a Lawyer in Utah [2026]: Courts, Fees, and Procedure
Source: https://filebankruptcywithoutlawyer.com/states/utah.html

← filebankruptcywithoutlawyer.com home

File Bankruptcy Without a Lawyer in Utah [2026]: Courts, Fees, and Procedure

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Utah residents.

Filing Bankruptcy Pro Se in Utah - Quick Orientation

Bankruptcy is federal. All Utah pro se filings go to a federal bankruptcy court, not a state court. You retain the 28 U.S.C. Section 1654 right to self-representation for individual cases (Chapter 7 and Chapter 13). Corporations and LLCs cannot file pro se per Rowland.

ItemUtah Detail

Bankruptcy districtsDistrict of Utah

Main courthouses350 S. Main St., Salt Lake City, UT 84101

Filing notesSingle district; SLC courthouse.

Chapter 7 filing fee$338 (2026)

Chapter 13 filing fee$313 (2026)

Chapter 11 filing fee$1,738 (consumer)

Venue - Where to File in Utah

Federal bankruptcy venue is governed by 28 U.S.C. Section 1408. File in the district where you have:

Domicile, residence, or principal place of business for the greater part of the 180 days immediately preceding filing, OR

Principal assets for the same period, OR

An affiliated pending case.

Utah venue note: Single district; SLC courthouse.

Utah Filing Fees (2026) and Fee Waivers

ChapterFiling FeeMiscellaneous

Chapter 7$338Waiver possible if income < 150% of poverty line (Form 103B)

Chapter 13$313Installment payments available (up to 4 per Rule 1006)

Chapter 11 (consumer)$1,738No waiver; installments possible

Chapter 12 (family farmer)$278Installments possible

Credit counseling$15-$50Pre-filing, 180-day validity, sliding scale available

Debtor education$15-$50Post-filing, pre-discharge

Additional fees (amendments, motions, reopening) are set by the U.S. Judicial Conference and published on uscourts.gov.

Utah E-Filing vs Paper Filing for Pro Se

Most Utah bankruptcy courts require paper filing for pro se debtors. CM/ECF (the electronic filing system) is generally reserved for licensed attorneys admitted to the district, though some districts offer limited pro se e-filing with pre-approval.

Practical Utah pro se filing workflow:

Download all national Official Forms from uscourts.gov.

Download the Utah district's Local Rules and local forms from the district's website.

Complete forms. Wet-ink signature on originals where required.

Make 3 copies (court, trustee, your file).

Pay the filing fee (cashier's check, money order, or in-person credit card if court accepts).

File in person or by mail to the clerk's office at one of the courthouses above.

See DIY bankruptcy walkthrough.

Required Forms for Utah Pro Se Filing

Every pro se Chapter 7 or 13 filing in Utah includes the following minimum set:

Voluntary Petition - Form 101 (individual) or 201 (entity, but pro se not allowed).

Schedules A/B through J - assets, debts, income, expenses.

Statement of Financial Affairs - Form 107.

Means Test - Form 122A-1 (Chapter 7) or 122C-1 (Chapter 13).

Statement of Intention - Form 108 (Chapter 7 only).

Chapter 13 Plan - Form 113 (Chapter 13 only).

Credit counseling certificate - dated within 180 days before filing.

Pay stubs - 60 days before filing (or Form 121 certification if none).

Tax return - most recent year's federal tax return; must be provided to the trustee at least 7 days before 341 meeting.

Creditor matrix - mailing addresses in the court's required format.

Utah districts may require local cover sheets and additional local forms. See Chapter 7 checklist and Chapter 13 checklist.

Utah 341 Meeting of Creditors

After filing, the court sets a 341 meeting (meeting of creditors) 20-40 days out. In Utah:

Attendance is mandatory. Missing the 341 is a leading cause of dismissal.

Format varies. Many Utah districts now use telephonic or video 341 meetings post-2020; some have returned to in-person. Check the notice carefully.

You answer under oath. The trustee asks standard questions about your schedules, income, and financial situation.

Duration: Typically 5-15 minutes for a no-asset Chapter 7; longer for contested matters or Chapter 13.

Bring photo ID and Social Security card (or W-2 showing SSN).

Bankruptcy Petition Preparers (BPPs) in Utah

BPPs are non-lawyers who type bankruptcy petitions for a fee under 11 U.S.C. Section 110. In Utah:

A BPP may type the forms you direct but cannot advise you on the law.

BPP fees are regulated; in most districts capped at $200-$225.

The BPP must sign the petition and disclose their identity (name, address, SSN or EIN).

BPPs are subject to sanctions for legal advice or for failing to disclose.

BPPs differ from licensed attorneys in that they cannot: (a) advise on exemptions, (b) advise on chapter choice, (c) represent you in court, (d) draft a Chapter 13 plan.

A BPP is useful if you can read and complete the forms yourself but want help with formatting. A BPP is not a substitute for legal advice. See full BPP guide.

Common Utah Pro Se Mistakes

Forgetting a creditor. Missing a creditor from the matrix can mean that debt is not discharged.

Undervaluing assets. The trustee will check; undervaluation looks like concealment.

Overlooking the Utah exemption election. Schedule C must affirmatively claim each exemption.

Missing the 60-day pay advice rule. Employer-issued pay stubs for 60 days pre-filing are required.

Filing without credit counseling certificate. The certificate must pre-date the petition.

Missing Rule 9037 redactions. Full SSNs, account numbers, and minor names trigger clerk alerts and must be re-filed.

See full mistake list.

Related Utah Resources

Chapter 13 pro se walkthrough

Common mistakes

Chapter 75498.1%1.9%

Chapter 136n/an/a

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Bankruptcy Petition Preparers (BPPs) in West Virginia

BPPs are non-lawyers who type bankruptcy petitions for a fee under 11 U.S.C. Section 110. In West Virginia:

A BPP may type the forms you direct but cannot advise you on the law.

BPP fees are regulated; in most districts capped at $200-$225.

The BPP must sign the petition and disclose their identity (name, address, SSN or EIN).

BPPs are subject to sanctions for legal advice or for failing to disclose.

BPPs differ from licensed attorneys in that they cannot: (a) advise on exemptions, (b) advise on chapter choice, (c) represent you in court, (d) draft a Chapter 13 plan.

A BPP is useful if you can read and complete the forms yourself but want help with formatting. A BPP is not a substitute for legal advice. See full BPP guide.

Common West Virginia Pro Se Mistakes

Forgetting a creditor. Missing a creditor from the matrix can mean that debt is not discharged.

Undervaluing assets. The trustee will check; undervaluation looks like concealment.

Overlooking the West Virginia exemption election. Schedule C must affirmatively claim each exemption.

Missing the 60-day pay advice rule. Employer-issued pay stubs for 60 days pre-filing are required.

Filing without credit counseling certificate. The certificate must pre-date the petition.

Missing Rule 9037 redactions. Full SSNs, account numbers, and minor names trigger clerk alerts and must be re-filed.

See full mistake list.

## File Bankruptcy Without a Lawyer in Wisconsin [2026]: Courts, Fees, and Procedure
Source: https://filebankruptcywithoutlawyer.com/states/wisconsin.html

← filebankruptcywithoutlawyer.com home

File Bankruptcy Without a Lawyer in Wisconsin [2026]: Courts, Fees, and Procedure

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Wisconsin residents.

Filing Bankruptcy Pro Se in Wisconsin - Quick Orientation

Bankruptcy is federal. All Wisconsin pro se filings go to a federal bankruptcy court, not a state court. You retain the 28 U.S.C. Section 1654 right to self-representation for individual cases (Chapter 7 and Chapter 13). Corporations and LLCs cannot file pro se per Rowland.

ItemWisconsin Detail

Bankruptcy districtsEastern and Western Districts

Main courthouses517 E. Wisconsin Ave, Milwaukee (WIE); 120 N. Henry St., Madison (WIW)

Filing notes2 districts.

Chapter 7 filing fee$338 (2026)

Chapter 13 filing fee$313 (2026)

Chapter 11 filing fee$1,738 (consumer)

Venue - Where to File in Wisconsin

Federal bankruptcy venue is governed by 28 U.S.C. Section 1408. File in the district where you have:

Domicile, residence, or principal place of business for the greater part of the 180 days immediately preceding filing, OR

Principal assets for the same period, OR

An affiliated pending case.

Wisconsin venue note: 2 districts.

Wisconsin Filing Fees (2026) and Fee Waivers

ChapterFiling FeeMiscellaneous

Chapter 7$338Waiver possible if income < 150% of poverty line (Form 103B)

Chapter 13$313Installment payments available (up to 4 per Rule 1006)

Chapter 11 (consumer)$1,738No waiver; installments possible

Chapter 12 (family farmer)$278Installments possible

Credit counseling$15-$50Pre-filing, 180-day validity, sliding scale available

Debtor education$15-$50Post-filing, pre-discharge

Additional fees (amendments, motions, reopening) are set by the U.S. Judicial Conference and published on uscourts.gov.

Wisconsin E-Filing vs Paper Filing for Pro Se

Most Wisconsin bankruptcy courts require paper filing for pro se debtors. CM/ECF (the electronic filing system) is generally reserved for licensed attorneys admitted to the district, though some districts offer limited pro se e-filing with pre-approval.

Practical Wisconsin pro se filing workflow:

Download all national Official Forms from uscourts.gov.

Download the Wisconsin district's Local Rules and local forms from the district's website.

Complete forms. Wet-ink signature on originals where required.

Make 3 copies (court, trustee, your file).

Pay the filing fee (cashier's check, money order, or in-person credit card if court accepts).

File in person or by mail to the clerk's office at one of the courthouses above.

See DIY bankruptcy walkthrough.

Required Forms for Wisconsin Pro Se Filing

Every pro se Chapter 7 or 13 filing in Wisconsin includes the following minimum set:

Voluntary Petition - Form 101 (individual) or 201 (entity, but pro se not allowed).

Schedules A/B through J - assets, debts, income, expenses.

Statement of Financial Affairs - Form 107.

Means Test - Form 122A-1 (Chapter 7) or 122C-1 (Chapter 13).

Statement of Intention - Form 108 (Chapter 7 only).

Chapter 13 Plan - Form 113 (Chapter 13 only).

Credit counseling certificate - dated within 180 days before filing.

Pay stubs - 60 days before filing (or Form 121 certification if none).

Tax return - most recent year's federal tax return; must be provided to the trustee at least 7 days before 341 meeting.

Creditor matrix - mailing addresses in the court's required format.

Wisconsin districts may require local cover sheets and additional local forms. See Chapter 7 checklist and Chapter 13 checklist.

Wisconsin 341 Meeting of Creditors

After filing, the court sets a 341 meeting (meeting of creditors) 20-40 days out. In Wisconsin:

Attendance is mandatory. Missing the 341 is a leading cause of dismissal.

Format varies. Many Wisconsin districts now use telephonic or video 341 meetings post-2020; some have returned to in-person. Check the notice carefully.

You answer under oath. The trustee asks standard questions about your schedules, income, and financial situation.

Duration: Typically 5-15 minutes for a no-asset Chapter 7; longer for contested matters or Chapter 13.

Bring photo ID and Social Security card (or W-2 showing SSN).

Wisconsin Federal Bankruptcy Data

Wisconsin's federal bankruptcy courts handle both attorney-filed and pro se cases under the same rules. The FJC numbers below give you a sense of Wisconsin docket scale and outcomes.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,541 consumer bankruptcy cases from Wisconsin's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 795399.4%0.4%

Chapter 1358848.1%51.9%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

BPPs are non-lawyers who type bankruptcy petitions for a fee under 11 U.S.C. Section 110. In Wisconsin:

A BPP may type the forms you direct but cannot advise you on the law.

BPP fees are regulated; in most districts capped at $200-$225.

The BPP must sign the petition and disclose their identity (name, address, SSN or EIN).

BPPs are subject to sanctions for legal advice or for failing to disclose.

BPPs differ from licensed attorneys in that they cannot: (a) advise on exemptions, (b) advise on chapter choice, (c) represent you in court, (d) draft a Chapter 13 plan.

A BPP is useful if you can read and complete the forms yourself but want help with formatting. A BPP is not a substitute for legal advice. See full BPP guide.

Forgetting a creditor. Missing a creditor from the matrix can mean that debt is not discharged.

Undervaluing assets. The trustee will check; undervaluation looks like concealment.

Overlooking the Wisconsin exemption election. Schedule C must affirmatively claim each exemption.

Missing the 60-day pay advice rule. Employer-issued pay stubs for 60 days pre-filing are required.

## Privacy Policy - filebankruptcywithoutlawyer.com
Source: https://filebankruptcywithoutlawyer.com/privacy.html

filebankruptcywithoutlawyer.com

Home
Privacy

Privacy Policy

How we handle your data. Short version: we don't sell it, share it, or use it for advertising.

Data We Collect

We use Google Analytics (GA4) to measure aggregate site traffic. This includes page views, session duration, approximate geographic region (country and city level), and device type. We do not collect names, email addresses, or personally identifiable information through analytics.

Aggregate event data from Google Analytics is also exported to Google BigQuery for research use. The BigQuery data is used only for internal trajectory analysis and network health reports, is not shared with third parties, and is not used for advertising.

What We Don't Do

We do not sell data. We do not run advertising. We do not collect financial information. We do not use retargeting. We do not share any user data with attorneys, law firms, creditors, debt collectors, or legal service providers.

Specifically, we do not enable Google Signals, Google Ads integration, User-ID collection, or any cross-device tracking feature in Google Analytics. GA4 operates in aggregate-traffic-measurement mode only on this site.

Cookies

We use only first-party cookies set by Google Analytics for aggregate traffic measurement. We do not use advertising cookies, tracking pixels, or third-party analytics cookies.

Third-Party Services

Google Analytics (GA4) - aggregate traffic measurement

Google BigQuery - aggregate event data warehouse for research use only; not shared, not used for advertising

Google Search Console - search query measurement (clicks, impressions, our own page rankings)

GitHub Pages - hosting

Contact Forms & Email

This site may link to contact forms or email addresses operated by the Open Bankruptcy Project. Any data you submit through those channels is handled under the Open Bankruptcy Project master privacy policy, which governs all sites in this network.

Children's Privacy

This site is not directed at children under 13. We do not knowingly collect information from children.

Data Retention

Analytics data is retained for 14 months per Google's standard retention settings. After that window, individual event data is automatically deleted by Google; aggregate report metrics remain available.

Your Rights

You may request deletion of any personal data we hold by contacting info@openbankruptcyproject.org. California residents have additional rights under CCPA. EU residents have additional rights under GDPR. All such requests are handled by the Open Bankruptcy Project.

Network Policy

This site is part of the Open Bankruptcy Project operated by the Open Bankruptcy Project, a 501(c)(3) public charity (EIN 41-5159631). The same privacy standards apply across every site in the network. The authoritative master policy is maintained at https://openbankruptcyproject.org/privacy.html.

Changes

We may update this policy from time to time. Changes are reflected on the master policy first and then mirrored across all network sites. Check the master policy for the most current version.

## About filebankruptcywithoutlawyer.com
Source: https://filebankruptcywithoutlawyer.com/about.html

filebankruptcywithoutlawyer.com

About

About filebankruptcywithoutlawyer.com

Part of the Open Bankruptcy Project operated by the Open Bankruptcy Project.

What This Site Is

filebankruptcywithoutlawyer.com is an educational resource operated by the Open Bankruptcy Project, a 501(c)(3) public charity (EIN 41-5159631). It's part of the Open Bankruptcy Project - a collection of free, public-interest sites that translate federal bankruptcy court data, statutes, and procedures into language ordinary people can use.

The Open Bankruptcy Project

The Open Bankruptcy Project builds free, open-source tools that make public bankruptcy court data accessible to the people it affects most - debtors, advocates, researchers, journalists, and policymakers. Every screening tool, analysis script, and dataset is published on GitHub. Anyone can audit, reproduce, or build upon the work without permission or payment.

Our research is derived primarily from the Federal Judicial Center's Integrated Database covering all federal bankruptcy filings 2008 through 2024, cross-referenced with PACER docket data via the Free Law Project's RECAP archive and independent court-scraping tooling. Methodology and source code are public.

What This Site Is Not

This site is not a law firm. We do not represent clients, file bankruptcy cases, or give legal advice. We do not receive referral fees, affiliate commissions, or advertising revenue. We do not sell data.

If you need legal advice about your specific situation, consult a licensed bankruptcy attorney in your state.

Research Contributions

Our research supports two accepted suggestions to the Federal Judicial Conference Advisory Committee on Bankruptcy Rules:

Suggestion 26-BK-3 - procedural screening for 11 U.S.C. § 1328(f) re-filing eligibility

Suggestion 26-BK-5 - Rule 9037 / Form 121 / Form 309E1 amendments addressing systematic unredacted Social Security number exposure on federal bankruptcy dockets

Contact

General inquiries, data requests, research collaboration, and media: info@openbankruptcyproject.org

Privacy and Data Handling

See our privacy policy for details. Short version: aggregate analytics only; no data sold, no advertising, no attorney referrals, no financial information collected.

## Additional FAQ Pages


### Common Questions - File Bankruptcy Without a Lawyer
Source: https://filebankruptcywithoutlawyer.com/paa/index.html

filebankruptcywithoutlawyer.com

Home
Questions

Common Questions

Clear, data-backed answers to the most frequently asked questions

Is it a bad idea to file bankruptcy without a lawyer?

What are the most common mistakes when filing bankruptcy pro se?

Recognizing and Avoiding Bankruptcy Mills

Bankruptcy mills are high-volume law firms that prioritize quantity over quality, often resulting in errors, missed deadlines, and inadequate representation. Red flags include heavily advertised low fees, minimal attorney contact, high paralegal-to-attorney ratios, and a lack of individualized attention to your case. The consequences of poor representation can be severe: missed exemptions, failure to address secured debts properly, and even case dismissal. Research any attorney thoroughly before hiring.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a bankruptcy mill?

A bankruptcy mill is a high-volume law firm that processes large numbers of bankruptcy cases using a template-driven approach with minimal attorney involvement. Warning signs include very low advertised fees, limited face time with your actual attorney, frequent errors in filings, and cases handled primarily by paralegals or non-attorney staff.

How much should a bankruptcy attorney cost?

Chapter 7 attorney fees typically range from $1,000 to $2,500 depending on case complexity and location. Chapter 13 fees are usually $2,500 to $5,000, often paid through the repayment plan. Be cautious of fees that seem unusually low, as they may indicate a mill-style practice that cuts corners on case quality.

How do I find a good bankruptcy attorney?

Look for an attorney who is board-certified in consumer bankruptcy or who focuses primarily on bankruptcy cases. Check reviews, ask about their caseload, and confirm that the attorney (not just a paralegal) will review your case. The NACBA (National Association of Consumer Bankruptcy Attorneys) and local bar associations offer referral services.

### Is it a bad idea to file bankruptcy without a lawyer? - File Bankruptcy Without a Lawyer
Source: https://filebankruptcywithoutlawyer.com/paa/is-it-a-bad-idea-to-file-bankruptcy-without-a-lawyer.html

Skip to content

filebankruptcywithoutlawyer.com

Home
Questions

Home › Common Questions › Is it a bad idea to file bankruptcy without a lawyer?

People Also Ask

Is it a bad idea to file bankruptcy without a lawyer?

It depends on your case complexity. For straightforward Chapter 7 cases with only unsecured debt, below-median income, and no significant assets, pro se filing is reasonable and can save $1,000-$2,500 in attorney fees. For Chapter 13, cases involving real estate, or cases with any complexity, hiring an attorney is strongly recommended.

The honest answer depends on your specific situation. Here is how to evaluate whether pro se filing makes sense for you.

Pro Se Is Reasonable When

You are filing Chapter 7 (not Chapter 13)

Your income is below the state median (simple means test)

You have only unsecured debts (credit cards, medical bills, personal loans)

You do not own real estate or have minimal home equity well within exemptions

You have not transferred property in the last 2-4 years

You are comfortable with detailed paperwork and following instructions precisely

You Should Hire an Attorney When

You are filing Chapter 13 (plan drafting requires legal expertise)

You own a home, especially with significant equity or arrears

You have a business or self-employment income

Your income is above the state median (complex means test)

You have made large payments to creditors or family members recently (preference issues)

You have tax debts, student loans, or other potentially non-dischargeable debts

A creditor has filed or threatened a fraud objection

The Risk-Reward Calculation

An attorney typically costs $1,000-$2,500 for Chapter 7. If hiring one protects a $20,000 homestead exemption or ensures a $50,000 debt is properly discharged, the return on investment is enormous. If your case is truly simple, the savings of pro se filing are meaningful - but be honest about your case's complexity.

### What are the most common mistakes when filing bankruptcy pro se? - File Bankruptcy Without a Lawyer
Source: https://filebankruptcywithoutlawyer.com/paa/what-are-the-most-common-mistakes-when-filing-bankruptcy-pro-se.html

Skip to content

filebankruptcywithoutlawyer.com

Home
Questions

Home › Common Questions › What are the most common mistakes when filing bankruptcy pro se?

People Also Ask

What are the most common mistakes when filing bankruptcy pro se?

The most common pro se mistakes are: failing to list all debts (unlisted debts may not be discharged), incorrectly valuing assets, missing exemption claims, not completing the means test properly, failing to attend the 341 meeting, not filing required credit counseling certificates, and missing deadlines for document submissions.

Knowing the common mistakes helps you avoid them. Here are the errors that most frequently cause problems for pro se filers.

Filing Errors

Incomplete debt schedules: You must list every creditor, even debts you want to keep paying. Unlisted debts may not be discharged in some jurisdictions.

Wrong asset values: Use current fair market value, not what you paid or what you think something should be worth. Overvaluing can cost you exemptions; undervaluing can trigger fraud concerns.

Missing exemptions: If you do not claim an exemption on Schedule C, the trustee can take the property. This is the most costly mistake pro se filers make.

Incorrect income calculation: The means test uses the 6-month lookback. Many pro se filers use current income instead of the required 6-month average.

Procedural Errors

Not filing the credit counseling certificate: Must be filed within 14 days of the petition or the case is dismissed

Missing the 341 meeting: Failure to appear typically results in case dismissal

Not filing the financial management course certificate: Discharge cannot be entered without it

Not responding to trustee requests: The trustee may request additional documents; failure to respond can lead to dismissal

Strategic Errors

Filing at the wrong time (bad means test window)

Not understanding preference payments (paying family members back before filing)

Transferring property before filing without understanding fraudulent transfer rules
